title: RBI Dollar Swap Scheme Drives 86% Surge in NRI Deposits to $60 Billion in Two Months
excerpt: India's central bank is absorbing hedging costs and allowing leverage of up to 19 times on FCNR(B) deposits, offering NRIs a rare high-yield window on dollar savings.
body:
• Outstanding FCNR(B) deposits surged 86% from $32.56 billion to $60.55 billion in under two months after the RBI launched a concessional swap facility on June 5, 2026.
  • The RBI absorbs the full hedging cost for banks, and some lenders are offering interest rates as high as 7.5% on dollar deposits — well above domestic deposit rates.
  • Banks are offering leverage of 9 to 19 times on these deposits, meaning an NRI with a $1 million deposit could invest up to $10 million or more at attractive rates.
  • The scheme targets $40-50 billion in inflows by September 30 and is designed to strengthen India's forex reserves amid global uncertainties.

Record Inflows Under RBI's Swap Window

The Reserve Bank of India's special concessional swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits has triggered a sharp surge in overseas foreign currency inflows, with outstanding deposits nearly doubling in less than two months. According to RBI's latest bank-wise data, FCNR(B) deposits climbed from $32.56 billion on June 5 — the day the scheme was announced — to $60.55 billion by July 30, an increase of roughly $28 billion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=hs2Pgh4v7m4

The facility was operationalized on June 8 with the objective of strengthening India's balance of payments and encouraging foreign currency inflows amid heightened global uncertainties, including the West Asia conflict. Under the scheme, the RBI provides buy-sell dollar swaps at par for fresh FCNR(B) deposits of three to five years duration, absorbing the full hedging cost that banks would otherwise bear.

"The forex inflow numbers via FCNR(B) deposits are very encouraging. Frankly, I would have expected a much lower figure. The official target is around US$40-50 billion, and mobilising US$17.4 billion in such a short period is a very good start."

— Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda

How the Scheme Works for NRIs

An FCNR(B) deposit allows Non-Resident Indians to park foreign income in India in the original currency, shielding them from exchange rate risk. The principal and interest are fully repatriable, giving NRIs flexibility to transfer savings back to overseas accounts.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2089216619897934159

What makes the current scheme particularly attractive is a combination of higher rates and leverage. The RBI removed interest rate ceilings on June 17, and some banks are now offering as much as 7.5% on dollar deposits — significantly above prevailing US deposit rates. The leverage component, permitted through RBI guidelines issued on June 23, allows customers to take loans against their deposits at ratios ranging from 9 to 19 times, according to Bloomberg and banking sources cited by The Hindu BusinessLine.

For an NRI depositing $1 million, borrowing $9 million against it at current leverage ratios would allow a $10 million investment earning 7.5% on the full amount. Brokerage house Jefferies noted that leverage was crucial to the scheme's success, drawing parallels with a similar 2013 program that also relied heavily on leveraged deposits.

Bank-Level Performance

State Bank of India remained the largest mobilizer, with outstanding FCNR(B) deposits rising from $9.70 billion to $13.82 billion. Among private sector banks, ICICI Bank recorded the sharpest increase — from $2.37 billion to $6.06 billion. HDFC Bank's deposits grew from $4.02 billion to $5.42 billion, while Axis Bank rose from $3.08 billion to $4.67 billion.

Foreign banks saw even more dramatic growth. HSBC's FCNR(B) deposits jumped from $120 million to $6.26 billion, while Standard Chartered mobilized $1.86 billion after having no outstanding FCNR(B) deposits at the start of the period.

Risks and Concerns

Not everyone is optimistic about the scheme's long-term implications. In an analysis published by The Hindu BusinessLine, academics from the National Institute of Bank Management and IIM Ahmedabad warned that the RBI is effectively increasing its short dollar position and creating contingent foreign currency liabilities.

Former RBI Deputy Governor SS Tarapore once called providing exchange rate guarantees a "sin" for central banks. The current scheme, critics argue, amounts to the RBI securing present stability while mortgaging future dollar commitments — every dollar swapped today must be returned in five years.

As Indian banks compete for dollar funding in global markets to support leveraged structures, borrowing costs are being pushed higher. The scheme also adds to the RBI's already inflated short forward commitments, which amount to roughly 20% of foreign currency assets.

What's Next

The FCNR(B) swap window remains open until September 30, with concessional swaps for overseas foreign currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings available until December 31, 2026. Bankers expect the pace of inflows to moderate somewhat, with incremental deposits increasingly dependent on leveraged structures.

For NRIs in the US and other markets, the window presents a time-limited opportunity to earn significantly higher returns on dollar savings through Indian banks, though the one-year lock-in and leverage risks deserve careful consideration.
nri_angle: NRIs in the US and other countries can earn significantly higher returns on dollar savings through the FCNR(B) scheme, with leverage and RBI-backed hedging making it a rare opportunity.
